newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Sept retail sales jump not proof of a pick-up.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Sept retail sales jump not proof of a pick-up.

text.p: A surprise jump in U.S. September retail sales was coupled with a slashing of the August figure and not enough to prove consumer demand has escaped its summer doldrums, economists said on Friday.
"We got a bit of unexpected strength in autos, but apart from that things don't look too good. I think consumer demand looks fairly sluggish," said David Sloan, domestic economist at I.D.E.A.
"Most of the gains in ex-auto retail sales were in food which is not likely to make a trend," he added.
The U.S. Department of Commerce reported a 0.7 percent rise in September retail sales, well above economists' consensus forecast for a 0.2 percent gain.
Meanwhile, the August figure underwent a sharp downward revision, registering a 0.2 percent drop versus a previously reported 0.2 percent gain.

Excluding the mercurial auto component, September sales jumped 0.4 percent, compared to a revised 0.5 percent fall in August which was the largest drop since October 1995, the Commerce Department said. Economists had expected a 0.3 percent ex-autos rise in September.
U.S. debt and equity markets rallied on the sales data which was coupled with the release of a subdued September producer price report.
The benchmark 30-year long bond gained half a point, trading up 23/32 to 99 flat at 0925 EDT/1325 GMT.

"I'm a little surprised the (Treasury) market is this euphoric over the downward revision to August. I think that is openly a mistake," said Michael Strauss, chief economist at Yamaichi International (America) Inc.
"The more important issue is that we are seeing a better spending pattern already in September," he added.
Strauss had forecast a 0.6 percent gain in September sales, on the high-end of Wall Street forecasts, and predicts a pick-up in consumer demand this fall.
However, most economists remained skeptical and stressed that consumer spending slowed considerably in the third quarter compared to the first half of 1996.
"It will probably come in near one percent in the second half," said Cheryl Katz, senior economist at Merrill Lynch.
The annualized growth rate of consumer spending at the end of the second quarter was a healthy 3.5 percent, well above the long-term trend of 2.0 percent, analysts said.
"The Federal Reserve certainly has noted that consumer spending was subdued in the third quarter," Sloan said.
In the September data, food stores sales drove the headline number above expectations, said Matthew Alexy, chief markets strategist at CS First Boston Corp.
The grocery store and food store components both rose 1.2 percent in September compared to 0.5 percent falls in August.

Also, auto sales steamed ahead to a 1.7 percent gain versus a 0.5 percent gain in August. This surprised some as the sale of domestic light vehicles dropped substantially to 13.2 million cars on a seasonally adjusted annual rate in September, versus 14.0 million in August, analysts said.
The opposite was evidenced in August when the auto component was flat even though unit sales surged, economists said, adding the disparity was due to seasonal adjustment factors.
